title: Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization

paper.title: Skill ∞ \infty : Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system also improves the way it improves, is a long-standing aspiration on the path to AGI.
Language agents increasingly store procedural knowledge in reusable skills.
Optimizing skills offers a direct way to achieve RSI, because the optimization procedure itself can be encoded as a skill.
Existing skill optimizers, however, follow a hand-designed procedure.
Even methods that evolve a meta-skill confine it to a fixed pipeline and relearn it for each task.
We present Skill ∞ \infty , which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself using the same procedure.
The optimization is agent-led.
The meta agent diagnoses execution traces, proposes candidates, requests independent reviews, and allocates the search budget.
The meta-skill defines these steps, allowing self-improvement to rewrite them.
This meta-skill is also decoupled from task skills, refined on multiple skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across diverse domains.
As in deployment, skills at both levels are standard packages loaded through native skill discovery.
On 83 SkillsBench tasks, Skill ∞ \infty reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to a system that improves not only its performance on tasks but also the procedure that produces these improvements ( Yudkowsky, 2007 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Because each gain can then accelerate the next, RSI has figured prominently in visions of artificial general intelligence (AGI), from the intelligence explosion envisioned by Good (1966) to Gödel machines ( Schmidhuber, 2003 ) . More recently, skills have emerged as a common format for capturing the reusable procedural knowledge of language agents ( Anthropic, 2025b ) . This format can also encode the procedure that optimizes skills. Skills can thus encode both the target of improvement and the procedure that improves it, making skill optimization a direct and interpretable way to achieve RSI. Skills also serve as a harness-agnostic medium for RSI, since Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025a ) , Codex ( OpenAI, 2025 ) , and OpenCode ( Anomaly, 2025 ) all load them through the same open specification ( Agent Skills, 2025 ) . To realize this potential, skill optimization must improve not only skills but also the procedure that optimizes them. Recent approaches such as SkillOpt ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , CoEvoSkills ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and SkillEvolver ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) already optimize skills from execution feedback. Despite differences in what they edit and how they verify candidates, these methods share one design choice. The optimizer follows a hand-designed procedure, and what it learns while optimizing one skill does not transfer to the next. MetaSkill-Evolve ( Wang et al., 2026b ) goes a step further: each search branch carries a meta-skill that configures the five agents of its pipeline, and the same pipeline refines this meta-skill. However, the pipeline’s roles and wiring remain fixed, and each meta-skill is bound to the task skill it evolves with. Some methods also optimize skills in a setting that differs from deployment ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . They inject the skill or prompt the agent to load it, so optimization never tests whether the agent would load the skill on its own. We believe that an optimizer that improves skills but not its own procedure will eventually stagnate. RSI targets exactly this limitation. In this work, we propose Skill ∞ \infty , a framework for recursively self-improving skill optimization. A meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and applies the same procedure to the meta-skill itself . The “ ∞ \infty ” in Skill ∞ \infty stands for two loops that meet at the meta-skill and feed into each other, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Optimization in Skill ∞ \infty is agent-led : in each iteration, the meta agent diagnoses the parent skill from execution traces, proposes and evaluates candidates within the search budget, submits each candidate to an independent reviewer, and selects the next parent. Self-improvement of the meta-skill refines this procedure, which in turn optimizes task skills more effectively. We further decouple the meta-skill from task skills. The meta-skill is refined on a set of skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize diverse task skills. This decoupling amortizes the cost of self-improvement over task skill optimization. Skills at both levels are also provided to agents through native skill discovery , as in deployment. We neither inject a skill nor prompt an agent to load one. Agents see only a skill’s name and description and decide whether to load it. The description is therefore also included in the scope of optimization. We evaluate Skill ∞ \infty on 83 agentic tasks from SkillsBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) , spanning eight domains, and on GPU kernel optimization from KernelBench ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ) . In the main comparison, all methods share the Codex CLI ( OpenAI, 2025 ) as the harness and GPT-6 Luna ( OpenAI, 2026b ) as the backbone model. On SkillsBench, Skill ∞ \infty reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver, and on KernelBench it reaches a mean speedup of 1.62. Without the self-improvement of the meta-skill, the pass rate falls to 55.9%. Skill ∞ \infty still outperforms human-curated skills when the backbone model or the harness is replaced. Case studies in Appendix C show that self-improvement changes how the meta agent acts, not only the wording of its instructions.

sections.heading: Recursive Self-Improvement
sections.text: The idea of RSI dates back to the argument for an intelligence explosion ( Good, 1966 ) . Gödel machines ( Schmidhuber, 2003 ) later formalized it as a program that rewrites its own code once a rewrite is proven useful. Long a vision of AGI, RSI has since been partly realized in agents built on language models. STOP ( Zelikman et al., 2024 ) runs a code-improving scaffold on its own code but notes that this is not full RSI, because the language model itself is not altered. Research on self-evolving agents ( Gao et al., 2026 ) has introduced systems that rewrite their own logic or code ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2026a ) or search over agent designs ( Hu et al., 2025 ) . More recent systems make the meta-level modification procedure itself editable ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) or compose data, harness, and model updates ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . R 2 Flow ( Zhang et al., 2026e ) trains a policy that orchestrates a skill library and commits verified edits to it. These systems implement the optimizer as a program or a trained policy. Skill ∞ \infty , however, encodes the optimizer’s procedure as a skill, which makes its recursive self-improvement direct, interpretable, and harness-agnostic.

sections.heading: Agent Skills and Skill Optimization
sections.text: Agent skills package reusable procedures as portable directories that agents load on demand ( Anthropic, 2025b ; Agent Skills, 2025 ; Xu and Yan, 2026 ) . This format has precedents in skill libraries, induced workflows, and programmatic web skills ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . A growing line of work learns skills from experience ( Ni et al., 2026 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) or optimizes them from execution feedback ( Alzubi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Tian et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . SkillEvolver ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) writes its optimization procedure as a fixed meta-skill that audits candidate skills in separate agents. Some methods go further and operate at the meta level, evolving meta-skills that guide skill optimization ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ) , multi-agent system design ( Lin et al., 2026a ) , or context engineering ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . These methods still evolve the meta-skill with a hand-designed procedure. MetaSkill-Evolve ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , for instance, fixes the roles and wiring of its five-agent pipeline and binds each meta-skill to the task skill it evolves with. Skill ∞ \infty instead writes an agent-led optimization procedure into the meta-skill and refines it through self-improvement on several skill optimization tasks. Decoupled from task skills, the same meta-skill then optimizes diverse task skills.

sections.heading: Prompt and Context Optimization
sections.text: Skill optimization builds on prompt optimization. Early methods select instructions that a language model proposes ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) or evolve populations of prompts ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Fernando et al., 2024 ) . Subsequent methods optimize compound systems of model calls ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2025 ; Khattab et al., 2024 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , accumulate strategies in evolving contexts ( Suzgun et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026f ) , or meta-learn system prompts that transfer across tasks ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Tao et al., 2026 ) . These methods optimize text that the surrounding system inserts into the model’s context. sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We first formalize skills, native skill discovery, and task skill optimization by a meta-skill. We then make the meta-skill an optimization target in its own right, so that a single agent-led procedure optimizes task skills and the meta-skill alike. Finally, we decouple the meta-skill from task skills and extend native skill discovery to both levels.

sections.heading: Skill Packages and Native Skill Discovery
sections.text: We adopt the Agent Skills specification ( Agent Skills, 2025 ) , an open format through which agents across harnesses share reusable procedural knowledge. A skill package is a directory built around the SKILL.md file. The front matter of SKILL.md declares the skill’s name and description, while the body holds the instructions. The package may also bundle scripts, reference files, and other resources that the instructions invoke or cite. With these resources, a skill can provide executable procedures and detailed conventions in addition to textual guidance. An agent loads skills in stages, following a design principle known as progressive disclosure ( Anthropic, 2025b ) . Initially, it sees only the name and description of each installed skill. For a skill it judges useful for the current task, it then loads the full instructions and opens the bundled resources as needed. A skill thus takes effect only when the agent activates it by loading its instructions. We term this mechanism native skill discovery because it is built into agent harnesses and underlies skill use during deployment.

sections.heading: Task Skill Optimization by a Meta-Skill
sections.text: Given a seed task skill s 0 s_{0} and a set of tasks T T , task skill optimization seeks a skill s ⋆ s^{\star} that maximizes the score on test tasks. Our optimizer is a meta agent built on the same harness and backbone model as the task agent rather than a stronger one. Its procedure is itself a skill: the meta agent follows a meta-skill m m , a skill package whose instructions describe how to optimize skills.

sections.heading: The Recursive Loop
sections.text: When the meta-skill improves itself, it is both the procedure that the meta agent follows and the target that this procedure optimizes. The meta agent thus diagnoses and revises this procedure while following it. The revised meta-skill is then evaluated on skill optimization tasks, where the optimizations it guides reveal whether it surpasses the predecessor. Such a loop makes self-improvement recursive, since improvements to the meta-skill are self-reinforcing. Each strengthens the procedure from which further improvements arise, yielding an increasingly capable meta-skill.

sections.heading: Anatomy of an Iteration
sections.text: We place the meta agent at the helm of skill optimization, following a meta-skill that is editable by self-improvement. Algorithm 1 outlines the procedure, and Figure 2 depicts one of its iterations. The meta agent first inspects the optimization history recorded in the archive. It then diagnoses the parent skill from the execution traces of its rollouts. Informed by this diagnosis, it creates one or two candidates from the parent, each justified by a proposal. The meta agent evaluates the candidates and submits each to an independent reviewer. Finally, it decides whether to continue and selects either the next parent or the optimized skill. sections.heading: Search as Reasoning
sections.text: Agent-led optimization entrusts the search to the meta agent’s reasoning rather than to a hand-designed heuristic driven by scores. A score reveals whether a candidate improved but not why, so the meta agent interprets it in light of the diagnoses and reviews recorded in the archive. The diagnoses can uncover a promising change that the score has yet to reflect, such as a tied candidate that makes progress on the failure it targets. Much as evolutionary search retains less fit candidates to escape local optima, the meta agent can build on such candidates instead of discarding them. It may likewise keep the parent when a candidate’s gain cannot be attributed to its change, or backtrack to an earlier skill when a line of revisions stalls. Beyond choosing parents, the meta agent decides which failures to address next, redirecting the search as new evidence emerges. In sum, search becomes reasoning about the failure modes of each target skill rather than a heuristic applied to all.

sections.heading: Independent Review
sections.text: Only candidates that pass an independent review are eligible for selection. The reviewer operates in an isolated context, shielded from both the meta agent’s deliberation and its partiality toward its own changes. The verdict rests solely on the parent and candidate packages, the proposal, and the supporting evidence. The reviewer rejects candidates that make no substantive change, that are never activated, or that are unusable as written. Any gain from such candidates can arise only by chance, and rejecting them prevents selection from mistaking noise for progress. For a meta-skill candidate, the reviewer further verifies that the core responsibilities of a meta-skill, including the review itself, remain intact.

sections.heading: Adaptive Budget Allocation
sections.text: The meta agent allocates the search budget itself, deciding how many candidates to create in each iteration and when to stop. The number of candidates per iteration sets the balance between exploration and exploitation. Several candidates probe alternative revisions side by side, whereas a single candidate pursues one line of revisions in depth. Across target skills, a fixed schedule would allocate the same budget regardless of how much headroom remains. The meta agent instead adapts its spending to each target skill, continuing while failures persist and stopping once the diagnosis finds little left to improve.

sections.heading: End-to-End RSI
sections.text: The steps of Algorithm 1 are encoded in the meta-skill rather than hard-coded, so the recursive loop of Section 3.2 can rewrite the procedure itself. Any part of the package, from the instructions to the bundled scripts, is open to revision. Freed from any predefined design space, the procedure can evolve beyond the foresight of human designers and realize its full potential. Self-improvement can remedy a weak step wherever it lies, even in the review and selection of candidates, which a fixed pipeline would leave untouched. Optimizing task skills reveals the shortcomings of the procedure, and each refinement in turn yields better task skills, rendering the two levels mutually reinforcing. To keep the mutual reinforcement genuine, scoring lies beyond the reach of self-improvement, so gains can arise only from better optimization, never from reward tampering.

sections.heading: 3.4 Decoupling Meta-Skill from Task Skills
sections.text: Skill ∞ \infty decouples the meta-skill from the task skills it optimizes. The meta agent first refines a seed meta-skill m 0 m_{0} into m ⋆ m^{\star} on a set of skill optimization tasks Q Q drawn from different domains. Each candidate meta-skill is scored by Equation 3 on the inner optimizations it guides, one for each q ∈ Q q\in Q within the inner budget B q B_{q} . The refined meta-skill m ⋆ m^{\star} then guides the optimization of each target task skill from its seed. This decoupling separates concerns: the meta-skill captures how to optimize skills, and each task skill how to solve its tasks. Averaging gains over Q Q , the meta score favors revisions that help across domains over those tailored to one. As a standard skill package, the refined meta-skill serves all task skills optimized afterwards, amortizing the cost of self-improvement across them.

sections.heading: 3.5 Native Skill Discovery at Both Levels
sections.text: Skills at both levels are installed in the harness’s standard skill location and loaded through native skill discovery, as in deployment. No skill is injected into a prompt, nor is any agent instructed to load one. Gains measured under these conditions need no injection to materialize in deployment. For task skills and the meta-skill alike, activation thus hinges on the description, which joins the instructions within the scope of optimization. Like any skill, the meta-skill is portable across harnesses that support native skill discovery.

We further locate where Skill ∞ \infty helps and measure how performance scales with the search budget and what optimization costs. sections.heading: Benchmarks
sections.text: SkillsBench quantifies how much skills improve agent performance across diverse agentic tasks by pairing each task with human-curated skills. We optimize task skills on the dataset released with SkillEvolver ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) and test them on its 83 SkillsBench tasks from eight domains. KernelBench challenges an agent to replace a PyTorch reference model with a faster implementation that computes the same outputs. Following SkillEvolver, we optimize one task skill shared across three level-3 problems whose reference models are a deep narrow MLP, ShuffleNet, and a GRU.

sections.heading: Baselines
sections.text: All baselines use the same harness and backbone model as Skill ∞ \infty . No skill and Human-curated evaluate the task agent without a skill and with the human-curated skills of SkillsBench, respectively. Self-generated asks the task agent to write its own skills before using them to solve the task ( Li et al., 2026a ) . SkillCreator authors a skill with Anthropic’s skill-creator ( Anthropic, 2025c ) , which CoEvoSkills ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) adapted to run without human interaction. SkillEvolver ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) uses its released meta-skill to author, deploy, and revise a skill over two rounds.

sections.heading: Configurations
sections.text: The main experiments use the Codex CLI ( OpenAI, 2025 ) with GPT-6 Luna ( OpenAI, 2026b ) at high reasoning effort, and Harbor ( Harbor Framework Team, 2026 ) executes the trials. Seed task skills are instantiated from the template in Appendix F , which identifies the task but carries no task-specific guidance. We measure the search budget in candidates and cap it at four per task skill. For self-improvement, the meta agent refines the seed meta-skill in Appendix G on skill optimization tasks drawn from different domains, with the budgets given in Appendix B . We choose tasks that the seed task skill has not saturated, since a saturated task offers no gain by which a stronger meta-skill could distinguish itself.

sections.heading: Metrics
sections.text: As in SkillEvolver, we evaluate performance on SkillsBench by avg@5, the pass rate over five trials per task. The metric counts a trial as passed when its reward is positive. On KernelBench, we report the correctness-weighted speedup, which is the speedup over the PyTorch reference for a correct implementation and zero for an incorrect one. All reported results are averaged over 5 independent runs.

sections.heading: KernelBench
sections.text: KernelBench probes the same procedure under an unbounded, continuous reward. Figure 3 shows the correctness-weighted speedups. Skill ∞ \infty reaches a mean speedup of 1.62, compared with 1.18 for SkillEvolver and 1.02 without a skill. On the deep narrow MLP and ShuffleNet, Skill ∞ \infty attains 1.87 and 1.97, against 1.12 and 1.39 for SkillEvolver, respectively. Beyond whether the agent succeeds, Skill ∞ \infty also improves how well it performs, nearly quadrupling the gain of SkillEvolver over the agent without a skill.

sections.heading: 4.3 Ablation of Self-Improvement
sections.text: Self-improvement refines the procedure that subsequently optimizes task skills. To quantify its contribution, we replace the refined meta-skill with its seed and report the result as Skill ∞ \infty w/o self-improvement in Table 1 . Even with the seed meta-skill, Skill ∞ \infty reaches an overall pass rate of 55.9%, which is higher than those of SkillEvolver and the other automatic baselines. The refined meta-skill improves the pass rate further to 60.7%. Self-improvement helps most in mathematics, media, and software engineering, by 24.0, 22.2, and 11.4 points, respectively. We attribute these gains to a stricter standard of evidence that self-improvement wrote into the meta-skill. The refined meta-skill confirms a fix only when the candidate’s rollout shows progress on the targeted failure, not when the revised skill merely mentions it. The agent-led procedure alone surpasses the automatic baselines, and by refining it, self-improvement places Skill ∞ \infty above human-curated skills.

sections.heading: Scaling the Search Budget
sections.text: We ask whether a larger budget yields further gains, given that the meta agent allocates the budget itself. We run this analysis on a subset of tasks, where the default budget substantially improves the seed task skill. We then optimize their task skills with budgets of one, two, and eight candidates under otherwise identical settings. As shown in Figure 5 , the pass rate rises with each doubling of the budget, from 47.5% with one candidate to 82.5% with eight. Even with a single candidate, the optimized task skills far exceed the agent without a skill (12.5%). The meta agent allocates each budget itself, so these gains require no retuning of the procedure. Agent-led optimization scales with the search budget.

sections.heading: Cost
sections.text: We measure cost by the tokens that all agents consume during optimization, as itemized in Appendix E . Optimizing a task skill with the refined meta-skill requires 8.7M input and 66k output tokens on average, close to 8.1M and 76k for SkillEvolver. The cost of self-improvement is amortized across all task skills optimized afterwards. Self-improvement consumes about as many tokens as eleven task skill optimizations. Spread over the 83 task skills, this cost adds less than 15% to each optimization, a share that shrinks with each further reuse of the meta-skill. By reusing its refined meta-skill, Skill ∞ \infty surpasses SkillEvolver at a comparable cost.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Skill optimizers have so far followed hand-designed procedures. Even methods that evolve a meta-skill fix the pipeline around it and relearn it for each task. We presented Skill ∞ \infty , which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving. A meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills, and the same agent-led procedure optimizes the meta-skill itself. The meta-skill, decoupled from task skills, is refined on skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across domains. At both levels, agents load their skills through native skill discovery, as in deployment. On SkillsBench, Skill ∞ \infty outperforms human-curated skills and SkillEvolver, and it improves kernel speedups on KernelBench. Encoding the optimizer’s procedure as a skill makes recursive self-improvement direct, interpretable, and harness-agnostic. We hope that this view invites further work on agents that improve the way they improve.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Skill ∞ \infty makes skill optimization recursively self-improving while the backbone model stays fixed. The resulting gains are therefore bounded by the expressiveness of skill packages. Both levels of optimization rely on automatic verifiers, since the meta score is computed from task rewards. Skill ∞ \infty therefore applies to domains in which such rewards can be computed reliably. Finally, agent-led optimization trades enforcement for flexibility. The meta agent follows its procedure rather than executing it as code. The effect of the meta-skill thus depends on how reliably the backbone model follows long instructions. No tool enforces this adherence, which rests instead on the meta-skill and on independent review.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: Optimized skills bundle instructions and executable scripts that agents follow with tool access, and an agent may activate them without user approval. We therefore recommend reviewing what these skills do and when they are activated before deploying them. Some SkillsBench tasks concern cybersecurity and are used only in the form the benchmark provides. SkillsBench is released under the Apache 2.0 license, and KernelBench and the dataset of SkillEvolver under the MIT license. We use these artifacts for research evaluation, consistent with their intended use.

sections.heading: Appendix A Skill-Utility Categories
sections.text: Following SkillEvolver, we assign tasks to skill-utility categories by the pass rates of No skill and Human-curated in Table 1 . Category A contains tasks on which No skill reaches a pass rate of at least 80%. Categories B1, B2, and B3 contain tasks on which the pass rate of No skill lies strictly between 0% and 80%. On these tasks, Human-curated achieves a higher, equal, or lower pass rate, respectively. Categories C1 and C2 contain tasks that No skill never passes. On these tasks, Human-curated reaches at least 40% or remains strictly between 0% and 40%, respectively. Category D contains tasks that neither method passes.

sections.heading: Appendix B Implementation Details
sections.text: The inner budget is two candidates per skill optimization task, and self-improvement may create at most four meta-skill candidates. In each iteration, the meta agent receives the request below. ⬇ Optimize the Task Skill in this workspace . Workspace : < absolute path > Complete optimization iteration < id >, write its decision , and then return .

sections.heading: The Meta-Skill Rewrites Its Selection Rule
sections.text: During self-improvement, the meta agent diagnosed the seed meta-skill from the inner optimizations it had guided. For the 3D scene task, the inner optimization had accepted two consecutive candidates while the verifier still reported the same link-geometry failure. It had also selected the second candidate, which only tied the parent. The meta agent located this weakness in the inspection and selection of evaluated candidates rather than in diagnosis. The candidate meta-skill it wrote requires checking the rollout of each tied or worse candidate for the targeted failure. A tied candidate can then be selected only when that rollout shows progress. The candidate improved the meta score from 0.55 to 0.83. In the next iteration, the meta agent followed this candidate and proposed a further change that tracks intermediate scores and verifier failures across candidates. The new candidate tied its parent. Applying the rule it had just written, the meta agent selected the tied candidate only after checking its inner optimization on the 3D scene task. There, the targeted failure had been addressed, and the task skill had reached a perfect score. Self-improvement then stopped after two further candidates and retained this candidate as the refined meta-skill. Across the 83 task skill optimizations, the refined meta-skill selected 54% of tied candidates, against 83% for the seed meta-skill. Self-improvement changes the behavior of the meta agent, not merely the text of its instructions.

sections.heading: A Task Skill Gains a Script
sections.text: For a SkillsBench task that exports the parts of a Three.js scene as OBJ files, the seed task skill fails all test trials. The meta agent attributed this failure to group ownership and coordinate transforms. It added an exporter script, wrote the ownership and transform rules into SKILL.md , and rewrote the description to specify the files the skill produces. Its proposal states a falsifying outcome in terms of the verifier’s check. The reviewer confirmed that the script exists and matches the documented interface before accepting the candidate. sections.heading: Appendix F Seed Task Skills
sections.text: All SkillsBench seed task skills are instantiated from a single template. Its description identifies the task, and its body prescribes only generic inspection, execution, and validation, with no knowledge specific to the task. The KernelBench task skill starts from a similar seed whose description refers to KernelBench tasks and whose body provides generic advice on profiling, correctness checks, and timing.

sections.heading: Appendix G Seed Meta-Skill
sections.text: The seed meta-skill is the starting point of self-improvement, and Skill ∞ \infty w/o self-improvement uses it to optimize all task skills. Its package contains SKILL.md , three reference files, and a Python script. SKILL.md defines the iteration of Algorithm 1 , the diagnostic procedure for both kinds of targets, and the scores. The reference files define the workspace and the decision record, the interface of the rollout and evaluation tools, and the review criteria. The script assembles the archive from the files in the workspace and initializes each candidate as a copy of its parent. SKILL.md and the reference files on the workspace and the tools are reproduced verbatim below. The front matter retains the package’s internal name. The names Meta Agent , Task Agent , and Reviewer Subagent in the files correspond to the meta agent, task agent, and reviewer in the paper, respectively. ⬇ — name : skill - self - evolver description : Optimize a Task Skill or this Meta Skill from rollout reports and evaluation results through candidate generation , scoring , review , and selection . — # Optimize skills Act as the Meta Agent in the supplied workspace . Read this skill ’ s instruction references before applying them . The [ workspace guide ]( references / workspace . md ) defines candidates , the archive , the candidate budget , and decisions . The [ evoctl interface ]( references / evoctl . md ) defines evaluation commands and their results . ## Complete one iteration 1. ** Inspect the archive .** Inspect the archive for the optimization target , parent , active iteration , prior outcomes , and remaining candidate budget . 2. ** Diagnose the parent .** Obtain its rollout with ‘ evoctl rollout ‘, and also the rollouts of its children from earlier iterations that scored no higher than it . Complete the [ diagnostic procedure ](# analyze - the - rollout ), then form falsifiable improvement hypotheses . 3. ** Create candidates .** Create one or two candidates in the active iteration within the remaining candidate budget , each containing a complete copy of the parent ’ s ‘ skill /‘ directory . Use the rollout diagnosis to improve the skill ’ s instructions and resources . Keep the skill ’ s name unchanged and its resource links valid . Write ‘ proposal . json ‘ in each candidate directory with the supporting observation , change , predicted effect , and falsifying outcome . A Meta Skill candidate preserves the [ required responsibilities ]( references / reviewer - policy . md # meta - skill - responsibilities ). 4. ** Evaluate candidates .** Evaluate ready candidates in parallel with ‘ evoctl evaluate ‘. Obtain and read each completed result . 5. ** Review evaluated candidates .** For each scored candidate , start a fresh Reviewer Subagent without inheriting your conversation . Provide absolute paths to the parent directory , the candidate directory , the candidate ’ s ‘ evaluation . json ‘, the parent ’ s ‘ rollout . md ‘, and the currently installed [ reviewer policy ]( references / reviewer - policy . md ). Run ready reviews alongside independent work . Wait for each reviewer to finish and read the candidate ’ s ‘ review . json ‘; use the same reviewer for corrections to that review . 6. ** Select and return .** After every submitted evaluation and the review of every scored candidate finish , refresh the archive . Compare the validation scores of the parent and reviewed candidates , considering reviews , history , and remaining candidate budget , then select whichever ‘ seed ‘ or ‘ accepted ‘ node you judge best . Select a candidate that only ties its parent when its change addresses a failure or requirement identified in the diagnosis . Write the active iteration ’ s [ decision . json ]( references / workspace . md # record - the - decision ), then return . ## Analyze the rollout Analyze the parent ’ s rollout to decide how to improve its skill . Treat the supplied reports , complete task packages including tests and reference solutions , and exported artifacts as read - only materials . Start with the rollout overview and follow relevant trajectory links . Use search and contextual reading to verify the actions and tool results behind an outcome , including subsequent recovery . Expand your reading when evidence is incomplete or conflicting . ### Task Skill 1. ** Understand the tasks and rewards .** Identify the skill ’ s supplied training tasks in the report . Read their instructions and tests / verifier source , including helpers that define the reward conditions . Inspect inputs and reference solutions as needed to understand the required behavior . 2. ** Analyze the execution .** Choose trials covering the relevant success and failure outcomes . Match the Task Agent ’ s actions , tool results , recovery attempts , and final outputs to the task requirements and verifier checks , and note avoidable detours . 3. ** Identify skill improvements .** Compare the Task Skill ’ s guidance with the Task Agent ’ s actual behavior . Identify missing , unclear , misleading , or unnecessary guidance , separating skill issues from execution , environment , and verifier issues . When the Task Agent rewrites or gets wrong a procedure that code can perform , provide that procedure as a script ; when it needs detailed conventions or data , provide them in a reference file linked from ‘ SKILL . md ‘. Propose reusable changes supported by the recorded evidence , preserving guidance that worked . ### Meta Skill 1. ** Locate optimization strengths and weaknesses .** Compare every supplied Task Skill ’ s initial and final validation scores , gains , and the Meta Skill ’ s training score . Select optimization trajectories that explain improvements , regressions , or missed opportunities . 2. ** Analyze the optimization process .** Trace how the Meta Agent and Reviewer Subagent used evidence , modified skills , and responded to feedback through their messages , actions , and tool results . Consult the Task Skill versions , available Task Skill rollouts , and node and iteration records linked from ‘ rollout . md ‘ as needed to verify their diagnoses and changes . 3. ** Identify Meta Skill improvements .** Relate the current Meta Skill ’ s instructions to the observed diagnosis , candidate generation , review , and selection . Determine which guidance would help the Meta Agent produce better Task Skills across the supplied tasks . ## Interpret scores The score , ‘ S ( skill ; evaluation_set )‘, aggregates performance on a fixed training or validation set . A gain is the difference between two scores under the same evaluation conditions . For a ** Task Skill **, the evaluation set contains tasks . The verifier produces a reward for each trial : “‘ text task_score ( s , t ) = mean of trial rewards for task t S ( s ; T ) = mean of task_score ( s , t ) over the supplied tasks t in T “‘ A ‘ timeout ‘ trial is scored on the artifacts present when the Task Agent reached its deadline ; trials without a verifier reward , including ‘ verifier_error ‘, count as zero when averaging trial rewards . For a ** Meta Skill **, the evaluation set contains skill optimization tasks . Each optimization task provides an initial Task Skill with its training and validation sets , and fixed optimization conditions . The Meta Agent uses the Meta Skill and its reviewer policy to optimize that Task Skill . Measure the improvement in its validation score : “‘ text gain ( m , q ) = S ( final Task Skill produced by m ; V_q ) - S ( initial Task Skill ; V_q ) S ( m ; Q ) = mean of gain ( m , q ) over the supplied skill optimization tasks q in Q “‘ Here ‘ V_q ‘ is the validation set for the Task Skill in optimization task ‘ q ‘. ⬇ # Optimization workspace ‘ WORKSPACE ‘ is the path supplied in the optimization request . ‘ context . json ‘ supplies ‘ optimization_target ‘ (‘ task_skill ‘ or ‘ meta_skill ‘) and this run ’ s candidate budget (‘ budget . max_candidates_per_run ‘). Each node holds one complete skill version . ‘ META_SKILL_DIR ‘ is the directory containing the installed ‘ SKILL . md ‘ you are running . Use that location for this skill ’ s scripts and references . “‘ text WORKSPACE / ├── context . json ├── tasks /< task - skill - id >/< task - id >/ # Training task packages ├── seed / │ ├── node . json │ ├── skill /< skill - name >/ │ ├── evaluation . json │ ├── rollout . md # Created by a rollout request │ └── rollout / └── iterations /000/ ├── candidates / i000 - c1 / │ ├── node . json │ ├── skill /< skill - name >/ │ ├── proposal . json │ ├── evaluation . json │ ├── review . json │ ├── rollout . md # Created by a rollout request │ └── rollout / └── decision . json “‘ The archive is derived from these files . Use the currently installed [ archive helper ](../ scripts / archive . py ), or read and organize the files directly . ## Task Skill rollout ‘ rollout . md ‘ summarizes training results and links to each task trial ’ s trajectory and supporting materials : “‘ text < node >/ rollout /< task - id >/< trial - index >/ ├── trajectory . md # Task Agent and subagent executions ├── verifier / # Recorded verifier results and diagnostics ├── artifacts / # Collected task outputs └── media / # Recorded images “‘ ## Meta Skill rollout ‘ rollout . md ‘ summarizes training results and links to the optimization trajectory and supporting materials for each Task Skill being optimized : “‘ text < node >/ rollout /< task - skill - id >/ ├── trajectory . md # Meta Agent and Reviewer Subagent executions ├── nodes /< node - id >/ # Task Skill , node records , and available rollout reports ├── iterations / # Per - iteration decisions and other recorded files └── media / # Recorded images “‘ ## Inspect the archive “‘ bash python META_SKILL_DIR / scripts / archive . py view – workspace WORKSPACE “‘ The archive view includes ‘ context ‘ from ‘ context . json ‘, nodes , scores , review status , generated - candidate counts , previous decisions , the active parent , ‘ candidate_root ‘, ‘ decision_path ‘, and ‘ remaining_candidates ‘. Creating a candidate consumes one candidate unit , including an unevaluated draft ; keep it in the archive . ## Create a candidate Choose a new directory under the active ‘ candidate_root ‘. Name it ‘ iNNN - cK ‘, where ‘ NNN ‘ is the iteration number and ‘ K ‘ is a positive candidate number . Use the active parent as the source for this iteration . “‘ bash python META_SKILL_DIR / scripts / archive . py create – workspace WORKSPACE – parent - dir PARENT_DIR – candidate - dir CANDIDATE_DIR “‘ The helper copies ‘ PARENT_DIR / skill /‘ to ‘ CANDIDATE_DIR / skill /‘, writes ‘ CANDIDATE_DIR / node . json ‘, and returns the candidate ’ s paths . Edit the copied skill and write ‘ CANDIDATE_DIR / proposal . json ‘. Node metadata has this form , with ‘ name ‘ identifying the directory under ‘ skill /‘: “‘ json { " node_id ": " i000 - c1 ", " parent_id ": " seed ", " iteration_id ": " i000 ", " name ": " skill - name " } “‘ A scored and reviewed candidate is ‘ accepted ‘ or ‘ rejected ‘ according to its review ; unresolved candidates are ‘ proposed ‘. The archive exposes each scored node ’ s ‘ validation_score ‘ from its ‘ evaluation . json ‘. ## Record the decision Write one ‘ decision . json ‘ in the active iteration : “‘ json { " action ": " continue ", " selected_node_id ": " i000 - c1 ", " reason ": " Evidence - grounded selection rationale and next optimization direction ." } “‘ Write exactly these three keys . Use ‘ continue ‘ when the run continues : ‘ selected_node_id ‘ becomes the next iteration ’ s parent . Use ‘ stop ‘ when the run ends , because the candidate budget is exhausted or you choose to finish : ‘ selected_node_id ‘ is the run ’ s final skill . If the candidate budget is later raised , a new iteration continues from that node . Ground the selection in the evidence in ‘ reason ‘: for ‘ continue ‘, add the next optimization direction ; for ‘ stop ‘, add why the search ends here . ⬇ # evoctl evaluation tools Successful commands return JSON . A correctable input error returns JSON with an ‘ error ‘ message string and a nonzero exit status . Keep a node ’ s skill unchanged once submitted to either command ; further edits belong in a new candidate . ## Obtain a rollout “‘ bash evoctl rollout – workspace WORKSPACE – node - dir NODE_DIR “‘ ‘ NODE_DIR ‘ identifies the skill node to run on the supplied training set . The response contains ‘ optimization_target ‘ ( as defined in the [ workspace guide ]( workspace . md )), ‘ node_id ‘, and ‘ rollout_path ‘. ‘ rollout_path ‘ points to ‘ NODE_DIR / rollout . md ‘, which provides the training score , skill activation , usage , elapsed time , and links to trajectories and supporting materials . Skill activation is reported as ‘ Yes ‘, ‘ No ‘, or ‘ Unknown ‘. ## Evaluate a candidate “‘ bash evoctl evaluate – workspace WORKSPACE – candidate - dir CANDIDATE_DIR “‘ ‘ CANDIDATE_DIR ‘ identifies a [ candidate node ]( workspace . md # create - a - candidate ). The command evaluates the candidate on the supplied validation set and returns JSON containing ‘ node_id ‘, ‘ validation_score ‘, and ‘ skill_activated ‘. The result is saved to ‘ CANDIDATE_DIR / evaluation . json ‘. ‘ skill_activated ‘ is ‘ true ‘ when activation is confirmed across the evaluated executions , ‘ false ‘ when any execution lacks activation , and ‘ null ‘ when unknown .

Language agents increasingly store procedural knowledge in reusable skills. Optimizing skills offers a direct way to achieve RSI, because the optimization procedure itself can be encoded as a skill. Existing skill optimizers, however, follow a hand-designed procedure. Even methods that evolve a meta-skill confine it to a fixed pipeline and relearn it for each task. We present Skill ∞ \infty , which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself using the same procedure. The optimization is agent-led. The meta agent diagnoses execution traces, proposes candidates, requests independent reviews, and allocates the search budget. The meta-skill defines these steps, allowing self-improvement to rewrite them. This meta-skill is also decoupled from task skills, refined on multiple skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across diverse domains. As in deployment, skills at both levels are standard packages loaded through native skill discovery. On 83 SkillsBench tasks, Skill ∞ \infty reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver. 1 Introduction m 0 m_{0} m 1 m_{1} m ⋆ m^{\star} s 0 s_{0} s 1 s_{1} s ⋆ s^{\star} Meta-skill optimizes itself Meta-skill optimizes task skills meta-skill/ SKILL.md § Complete one iteration § Analyze the rollout § Interpret scores references/ workspace.md evoctl.md reviewer-policy.md scripts/ archive.py Skill ∞ \infty : Prior methods: Optimizer Skill Hand-designed procedure Meta-skill Skill Evolving in a fixed pipeline Bound to one skill Figure 1: Recursively self-improving skill optimization. Center: the ∞ \infty shape shows the two loops of Skill ∞ \infty , which meet at the meta-skill. Each of its parts, from instructions to scripts, falls within the scope of self-improvement. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to a system that improves not only its performance on tasks but also the procedure that produces these improvements ( Yudkowsky, 2007 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Because each gain can then accelerate the next, RSI has figured prominently in visions of artificial general intelligence (AGI), from the intelligence explosion envisioned by Good (1966) to Gödel machines ( Schmidhuber, 2003 ) . More recently, skills have emerged as a common format for capturing the reusable procedural knowledge of language agents ( Anthropic, 2025b ) . This format can also encode the procedure that optimizes skills. Skills can thus encode both the target of improvement and the procedure that improves it, making skill optimization a direct and interpretable way to achieve RSI. Skills also serve as a harness-agnostic medium for RSI, since Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025a ) , Codex ( OpenAI, 2025 ) , and OpenCode ( Anomaly, 2025 ) all load them through the same open specification ( Agent Skills, 2025 ) . To realize this potential, skill optimization must improve not only skills but also the procedure that optimizes them. Recent approaches such as SkillOpt ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , CoEvoSkills ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and SkillEvolver ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) already optimize skills from execution feedback. Despite differences in what they edit and how they verify candidates, these methods share one design choice. The optimizer follows a hand-designed procedure, and what it learns while optimizing one skill does not transfer to the next. MetaSkill-Evolve ( Wang et al., 2026b ) goes a step further: each search branch carries a meta-skill that configures the five agents of its pipeline, and the same pipeline refines this meta-skill. However, the pipeline’s roles and wiring remain fixed, and each meta-skill is bound to the task skill it evolves with. Some methods also optimize skills in a setting that differs from deployment ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . They inject the skill or prompt the agent to load it, so optimization never tests whether the agent would load the skill on its own. We believe that an optimizer that improves skills but not its own procedure will eventually stagnate. RSI targets exactly this limitation. In this work, we propose Skill ∞ \infty , a framework for recursively self-improving skill optimization. A meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and applies the same procedure to the meta-skill itself . The “ ∞ \infty ” in Skill ∞ \infty stands for two loops that meet at the meta-skill and feed into each other, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Optimization in Skill ∞ \infty is agent-led : in each iteration, the meta agent diagnoses the parent skill from execution traces, proposes and evaluates candidates within the search budget, submits each candidate to an independent reviewer, and selects the next parent. Self-improvement of the meta-skill refines this procedure, which in turn optimizes task skills more effectively. We further decouple the meta-skill from task skills. The meta-skill is refined on a set of skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize diverse task skills. This decoupling amortizes the cost of self-improvement over task skill optimization. Skills at both levels are also provided to agents through native skill discovery , as in deployment. We neither inject a skill nor prompt an agent to load one. Agents see only a skill’s name and description and decide whether to load it. The description is therefore also included in the scope of optimization. We evaluate Skill ∞ \infty on 83 agentic tasks from SkillsBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) , spanning eight domains, and on GPU kernel optimization from KernelBench ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ) . In the main comparison, all methods share the Codex CLI ( OpenAI, 2025 ) as the harness and GPT-6 Luna ( OpenAI, 2026b ) as the backbone model. On SkillsBench, Skill ∞ \infty reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver, and on KernelBench it reaches a mean speedup of 1.62. Without the self-improvement of the meta-skill, the pass rate falls to 55.9%. Skill ∞ \infty still outperforms human-curated skills when the backbone model or the harness is replaced. Case studies in Appendix C show that self-improvement changes how the meta agent acts, not only the wording of its instructions. 2 Related Work Recursive Self-Improvement The idea of RSI dates back to the argument for an intelligence explosion ( Good, 1966 ) . Gödel machines ( Schmidhuber, 2003 ) later formalized it as a program that rewrites its own code once a rewrite is proven useful. Long a vision of AGI, RSI has since been partly realized in agents built on language models. STOP ( Zelikman et al., 2024 ) runs a code-improving scaffold on its own code but notes that this is not full RSI, because the language model itself is not altered. Research on self-evolving agents ( Gao et al., 2026 ) has introduced systems that rewrite their own logic or code ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2026a ) or search over agent designs ( Hu et al., 2025 ) . More recent systems make the meta-level modification procedure itself editable ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) or compose data, harness, and model updates ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . R 2 Flow ( Zhang et al., 2026e ) trains a policy that orchestrates a skill library and commits verified edits to it. These systems implement the optimizer as a program or a trained policy. Skill ∞ \infty , however, encodes the optimizer’s procedure as a skill, which makes its recursive self-improvement direct, interpretable, and harness-agnostic. Agent Skills and Skill Optimization Agent skills package reusable procedures as portable directories that agents load on demand ( Anthropic, 2025b ; Agent Skills, 2025 ; Xu and Yan, 2026 ) . This format has precedents in skill libraries, induced workflows, and programmatic web skills ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . A growing line of work learns skills from experience ( Ni et al., 2026 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) or optimizes them from execution feedback ( Alzubi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Tian et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . SkillEvolver ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) writes its optimization procedure as a fixed meta-skill that audits candidate skills in separate agents. Some methods go further and operate at the meta level, evolving meta-skills that guide skill optimization ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ) , multi-agent system design ( Lin et al., 2026a ) , or context engineering ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . These methods still evolve the meta-skill with a hand-designed procedure. MetaSkill-Evolve ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , for instance, fixes the roles and wiring of its five-agent pipeline and binds each meta-skill to the task skill it evolves with. Skill ∞ \infty instead writes an agent-led optimization procedure into the meta-skill and refines it through self-improvement on several skill optimization tasks. Decoupled from task skills, the same meta-skill then optimizes diverse task skills. Prompt and Context Optimization Skill optimization builds on prompt optimization. Early methods select instructions that a language model proposes ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) or evolve populations of prompts ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Fernando et al., 2024 ) . Subsequent methods optimize compound systems of model calls ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2025 ; Khattab et al., 2024 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , accumulate strategies in evolving contexts ( Suzgun et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026f ) , or meta-learn system prompts that transfer across tasks ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Tao et al., 2026 ) . These methods optimize text that the surrounding system inserts into the model’s context. The meta agent attributes a failed check to one action of the task agent and proposes an exporter script as the fix. 3 Method We first formalize skills, native skill discovery, and task skill optimization by a meta-skill. We then make the meta-skill an optimization target in its own right, so that a single agent-led procedure optimizes task skills and the meta-skill alike. Finally, we decouple the meta-skill from task skills and extend native skill discovery to both levels. 3.1 Preliminaries Skill Packages and Native Skill Discovery We adopt the Agent Skills specification ( Agent Skills, 2025 ) , an open format through which agents across harnesses share reusable procedural knowledge. A skill package is a directory built around the SKILL.md file. The front matter of SKILL.md declares the skill’s name and description, while the body holds the instructions. The package may also bundle scripts, reference files, and other resources that the instructions invoke or cite. With these resources, a skill can provide executable procedures and detailed conventions in addition to textual guidance. An agent loads skills in stages, following a design principle known as progressive disclosure ( Anthropic, 2025b ) . Initially, it sees only the name and description of each installed skill. For a skill it judges useful for the current task, it then loads the full instructions and opens the bundled resources as needed. A skill thus takes effect only when the agent activates it by loading its instructions. We term this mechanism native skill discovery because it is built into agent harnesses and underlies skill use during deployment. Tasks and Task Skills A task τ \tau consists of an instruction, an environment, and a verifier that returns a scalar reward for each trial , one execution by a task agent. A task agent is an agent harness with a backbone model and an installed task skill s s . The score of s s on a set of tasks T T is the mean reward over n n trials per task, macro-averaged across tasks: S ⁡ ( s , T ) = 1 | T | ​ ∑ τ ∈ T 1 n ​ ∑ j = 1 n r j ​ ( s , τ ) , S(s;T)=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{\tau\in T}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}r_{j}(s,\tau), (1) where r j ​ ( s , τ ) r_{j}(s,\tau) is the reward of the j j -th trial on task τ \tau with skill s s . Task Skill Optimization by a Meta-Skill Given a seed task skill s 0 s_{0} and a set of tasks T T , task skill optimization seeks a skill s ⋆ s^{\star} that maximizes the score on test tasks. Our optimizer is a meta agent built on the same harness and backbone model as the task agent rather than a stronger one. Its procedure is itself a skill: the meta agent follows a meta-skill m m , a skill package whose instructions describe how to optimize skills. 3.2 Recursively Self-Improving Skill Optimization Skill Optimization Tasks We make skill optimization recursively self-improving by optimizing the meta-skill with the same procedure that optimizes task skills. Just as a task skill is evaluated on tasks, a meta-skill is evaluated on skill optimization tasks . A skill optimization task q = ( s 0 q , T q , B q ) q=(s_{0}^{q},T_{q},B_{q}) asks the meta agent to optimize a seed task skill s 0 q s_{0}^{q} on tasks T q T_{q} within a search budget B q B_{q} . Following meta-skill m m , the meta agent produces an optimized task skill s q ⋆ ​ ( m ) s^{\star}_{q}(m) for q q . The reward of m m on q q is the gain of the optimized task skill over the seed: g ⁡ ( m , q ) = S ⁡ ( s q ⋆ ​ ( m ) , T q ) − S ⁡ ( s 0 q , T q ) . g(m,q)=S\big(s^{\star}_{q}(m);T_{q}\big)-S\big(s_{0}^{q};T_{q}\big). (2) The meta score of m m on a set of skill optimization tasks Q Q is the mean gain: S ⁡ ( m , Q ) = 1 | Q | ​ ∑ q ∈ Q g ⁡ ( m , q ) . S(m;Q)=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}g(m,q). (3) Skill optimization tasks and the meta score are the meta-level counterparts of tasks and the score. The agent-led procedure of Section 3.3 therefore applies directly to the meta-skill itself. The Recursive Loop When the meta-skill improves itself, it is both the procedure that the meta agent follows and the target that this procedure optimizes. The meta agent thus diagnoses and revises this procedure while following it. The revised meta-skill is then evaluated on skill optimization tasks, where the optimizations it guides reveal whether it surpasses the predecessor. Such a loop makes self-improvement recursive, since improvements to the meta-skill are self-reinforcing. Each strengthens the procedure from which further improvements arise, yielding an increasingly capable meta-skill. 3.3 Agent-Led Optimization Anatomy of an Iteration We place the meta agent at the helm of skill optimization, following a meta-skill that is editable by self-improvement. Algorithm 1 outlines the procedure, and Figure 2 depicts one of its iterations. The meta agent first inspects the optimization history recorded in the archive. It then diagnoses the parent skill from the execution traces of its rollouts. Informed by this diagnosis, it creates one or two candidates from the parent, each justified by a proposal. The meta agent evaluates the candidates and submits each to an independent reviewer. Finally, it decides whether to continue and selects either the next parent or the optimized skill. A score reveals whether a candidate improved but not why, so the meta agent interprets it in light of the diagnoses and reviews recorded in the archive. The diagnoses can uncover a promising change that the score has yet to reflect, such as a tied candidate that makes progress on the failure it targets. Much as evolutionary search retains less fit candidates to escape local optima, the meta agent can build on such candidates instead of discarding them. It may likewise keep the parent when a candidate’s gain cannot be attributed to its change, or backtrack to an earlier skill when a line of revisions stalls. Beyond choosing parents, the meta agent decides which failures to address next, redirecting the search as new evidence emerges. In sum, search becomes reasoning about the failure modes of each target skill rather than a heuristic applied to all. Independent Review Only candidates that pass an independent review are eligible for selection. The reviewer operates in an isolated context, shielded from both the meta agent’s deliberation and its partiality toward its own changes. The verdict rests solely on the parent and candidate packages, the proposal, and the supporting evidence. The reviewer rejects candidates that make no substantive change, that are never activated, or that are unusable as written. Any gain from such candidates can arise only by chance, and rejecting them prevents selection from mistaking noise for progress. For a meta-skill candidate, the reviewer further verifies that the core responsibilities of a meta-skill, including the review itself, remain intact. Adaptive Budget Allocation The meta agent allocates the search budget itself, deciding how many candidates to create in each iteration and when to stop. The number of candidates per iteration sets the balance between exploration and exploitation. Several candidates probe alternative revisions side by side, whereas a single candidate pursues one line of revisions in depth. Across target skills, a fixed schedule would allocate the same budget regardless of how much headroom remains. The meta agent instead adapts its spending to each target skill, continuing while failures persist and stopping once the diagnosis finds little left to improve. End-to-End RSI The steps of Algorithm 1 are encoded in the meta-skill rather than hard-coded, so the recursive loop of Section 3.2 can rewrite the procedure itself. Any part of the package, from the instructions to the bundled scripts, is open to revision. Freed from any predefined design space, the procedure can evolve beyond the foresight of human designers and realize its full potential. Self-improvement can remedy a weak step wherever it lies, even in the review and selection of candidates, which a fixed pipeline would leave untouched. Optimizing task skills reveals the shortcomings of the procedure, and each refinement in turn yields better task skills, rendering the two levels mutually reinforcing. To keep the mutual reinforcement genuine, scoring lies beyond the reach of self-improvement, so gains can arise only from better optimization, never from reward tampering. 3.4 Decoupling Meta-Skill from Task Skills Skill ∞ \infty decouples the meta-skill from the task skills it optimizes. The meta agent first refines a seed meta-skill m 0 m_{0} into m ⋆ m^{\star} on a set of skill optimization tasks Q Q drawn from different domains. Each candidate meta-skill is scored by Equation 3 on the inner optimizations it guides, one for each q ∈ Q q\in Q within the inner budget B q B_{q} . The refined meta-skill m ⋆ m^{\star} then guides the optimization of each target task skill from its seed. This decoupling separates concerns: the meta-skill captures how to optimize skills, and each task skill how to solve its tasks. Averaging gains over Q Q , the meta score favors revisions that help across domains over those tailored to one. As a standard skill package, the refined meta-skill serves all task skills optimized afterwards, amortizing the cost of self-improvement across them. 3.5 Native Skill Discovery at Both Levels Skills at both levels are installed in the harness’s standard skill location and loaded through native skill discovery, as in deployment. No skill is injected into a prompt, nor is any agent instructed to load one. Gains measured under these conditions need no injection to materialize in deployment. For task skills and the meta-skill alike, activation thus hinges on the description, which joins the instructions within the scope of optimization. Like any skill, the meta-skill is portable across harnesses that support native skill discovery. 4 Experiments We evaluate Skill ∞ \infty on SkillsBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) and KernelBench ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ) against baselines with and without skills. Beyond the main results, we ablate self-improvement and test generality across harnesses and models. We further locate where Skill ∞ \infty helps and measure how performance scales with the search budget and what optimization costs. Even methods that evolve a meta-skill fix the pipeline around it and relearn it for each task. We presented Skill ∞ \infty , which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving. A meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills, and the same agent-led procedure optimizes the meta-skill itself. The meta-skill, decoupled from task skills, is refined on skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across domains. At both levels, agents load their skills through native skill discovery, as in deployment. On SkillsBench, Skill ∞ \infty outperforms human-curated skills and SkillEvolver, and it improves kernel speedups on KernelBench. Encoding the optimizer’s procedure as a skill makes recursive self-improvement direct, interpretable, and harness-agnostic. We hope that this view invites further work on agents that improve the way they improve. Limitations Skill ∞ \infty makes skill optimization recursively self-improving while the backbone model stays fixed. The resulting gains are therefore bounded by the expressiveness of skill packages. Both levels of optimization rely on automatic verifiers, since the meta score is computed from task rewards. Skill ∞ \infty therefore applies to domains in which such rewards can be computed reliably. Finally, agent-led optimization trades enforcement for flexibility. The meta agent follows its procedure rather than executing it as code. The effect of the meta-skill thus depends on how reliably the backbone model follows long instructions. No tool enforces this adherence, which rests instead on the meta-skill and on independent review. Ethical Considerations Optimized skills bundle instructions and executable scripts that agents follow with tool access, and an agent may activate them without user approval. We therefore recommend reviewing what these skills do and when they are activated before deploying them. Some SkillsBench tasks concern cybersecurity and are used only in the form the benchmark provides. Appendix A Skill-Utility Categories Following SkillEvolver, we assign tasks to skill-utility categories by the pass rates of No skill and Human-curated in Table 1 . Category A contains tasks on which No skill reaches a pass rate of at least 80%. Categories B1, B2, and B3 contain tasks on which the pass rate of No skill lies strictly between 0% and 80%. Appendix C Case Studies The Meta-Skill Rewrites Its Selection Rule During self-improvement, the meta agent diagnosed the seed meta-skill from the inner optimizations it had guided. For the 3D scene task, the inner optimization had accepted two consecutive candidates while the verifier still reported the same link-geometry failure. It had also selected the second candidate, which only tied the parent. The meta agent located this weakness in the inspection and selection of evaluated candidates rather than in diagnosis. The candidate meta-skill it wrote requires checking the rollout of each tied or worse candidate for the targeted failure. A tied candidate can then be selected only when that rollout shows progress. The candidate improved the meta score from 0.55 to 0.83. In the next iteration, the meta agent followed this candidate and proposed a further change that tracks intermediate scores and verifier failures across candidates. The new candidate tied its parent. Applying the rule it had just written, the meta agent selected the tied candidate only after checking its inner optimization on the 3D scene task. There, the targeted failure had been addressed, and the task skill had reached a perfect score. Self-improvement then stopped after two further candidates and retained this candidate as the refined meta-skill. Across the 83 task skill optimizations, the refined meta-skill selected 54% of tied candidates, against 83% for the seed meta-skill. Self-improvement changes the behavior of the meta agent, not merely the text of its instructions.
